title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination
trick: Size the KV-versus-recurrent-state split and the admission cap from the average trajectory's footprint, route turns by trajectory label, admit more samples than environment slots, and dispatch tool jobs deepest-chain-first within 30-second arrival bands.
framing_stripped: Called 'inference-environment coordination' with a 'workload-aware capacity model', LBCH routing, routing-prefix (RP) scheduling, 'capacity separation' and 'Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS)'; it is (a) a one-scalar-per-workload rule for SGLang's mamba_full_memory_ratio and sample-concurrency knobs on a hybrid KDA+MLA model, derived by equating the number of trajectories each cache pool can hold (sec. 3.1); (b) consistent hashing with bounded loads (Mirrokni et al. 2016) applied per turn with the trajectory id as the key (sec. 3.2), plus a two-tier queue sort that only runs the radix prefix lookup for requests whose trajectory was recently batched (sec. 3.3); (c) two separate concurrency limits in the agent harness instead of one (sec. 4.1); and (d) a fixed lexicographic priority on pending tool jobs, arrival band first, then most completed turns, then shortest mean inference time, then FCFS (sec. 4.2). The 65.0% headline is almost entirely (c) against a harness that ran three tasks at a time on eight GPUs (Table 3, Table A2); CAAS itself is worth 1.9-3.5% in replay and 3.1-8.5% live.
method_equations: Hybrid-cache capacity model (sec. 3.1.1-3.1.2). $M$ is the GPU memory left for the KV-cache and recurrent-state pools after weights and runtime reservations; $M_{\mathrm{kv}}$ and $M_{\mathrm{state}}$ the two pool sizes; $r = M_{\mathrm{state}}/M_{\mathrm{kv}}$ the split, so $M_{\mathrm{state}}(r) = M\,r/(1+r)$ and $M_{\mathrm{kv}}(r) = M/(1+r)$ (eq. 1). For workload $\mathcal{D}$ the per-trajectory footprints are $$F_{\mathrm{kv}}(\mathcal{D}) = L_{\mathrm{kv}}(\mathcal{D})\,c_{\mathrm{kv}}, \qquad F_{\mathrm{state}} = S_{\mathrm{state}}\,c_{\mathrm{state}},$$ (eq. 2) where $L_{\mathrm{kv}}(\mathcal{D})$ is the mean number of KV entries a complete trajectory needs at its final turn (from historical trajectories of the same benchmark on a nearby checkpoint), $S_{\mathrm{state}}$ the recurrent-state slots per request (one state per trajectory is kept, sec. 3.1, via mamba_max_states_per_path=1, sec. 3.4), and $c_{\mathrm{kv}}, c_{\mathrm{state}}$ their unit memory costs. Pool residency $C_{\mathrm{kv}}(r;\mathcal{D}) = M_{\mathrm{kv}}(r)/F_{\mathrm{kv}}(\mathcal{D})$ and $C_{\mathrm{state}}(r) = M_{\mathrm{state}}(r)/F_{\mathrm{state}}$ (eq. 3); joint residency $C(r;\mathcal{D}) = \min\{C_{\mathrm{kv}}, C_{\mathrm{state}}\}$ (eq. 4). Equating the two gives the balancing ratio $$r^{\mathrm{bal}}(\mathcal{D}) = \frac{F_{\mathrm{state}}}{F_{\mathrm{kv}}(\mathcal{D})} = \frac{S_{\mathrm{state}}\,c_{\mathrm{state}}}{L_{\mathrm{kv}}(\mathcal{D})\,c_{\mathrm{kv}}}$$ (eq. 6) and $C(r^{\mathrm{bal}};\mathcal{D}) = M/(F_{\mathrm{kv}}(\mathcal{D}) + F_{\mathrm{state}})$ (eq. 7). With $\hat r$ the chosen ratio (model-derived or locally calibrated) and $W$ homogeneous workers, the reference sample concurrency is $$C_I^{\star}(\hat r;\mathcal{D}) = W\,\lfloor C(\hat r;\mathcal{D}) \rfloor$$ (eq. 8), 'not a hard limit'. Measured: $r^{\mathrm{bal}} = 0.09$ (SWE), $2.26$ (BFCL), $0.10$ (WideSearch), $C_{\mathrm{ref}} = 98, 859, 98$ per TP4 worker (sec. 5.2.1); best measured ratios $0.135$, $1.13$, $0.15$ (Fig. 4), so the model is off by $1.5\times$, $0.5\times$, $1.5\times$ and the makespan gap to the best cell is described only as 'close' (Fig. 3 values not in text). Raising $C_S$ from 147 to 157 (SWE), 644 to 859 (BFCL), 123 to 147 (WideSearch) multiplies new-prefill work by about 11, 3 and 9 and raises makespan (Figs. 4-5). LBCH routing (sec. 3.2, Alg. 1): trajectory $k$ carries label $\kappa_k$, hashed to a ring; home worker $h(\kappa_k)$; $L(w)$ in-flight requests on worker $w$, $L_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_w L(w)$; worker eligible when $$L(w) \le \frac{L_{\mathrm{tot}}+1}{W}\,\alpha,$$ (eq. 9) $\alpha \ge 1$ the load-bound factor ($\alpha = 1.25$ in all experiments); first eligible worker clockwise from home, else home. RP scheduling (sec. 3.3, Alg. 2): per worker, label set $\mathcal{A}$ of the $C_{\mathcal{A}}$ most recently batched trajectory labels (LRU; default $C_{\mathcal{A}} = \lfloor C(\hat r;\mathcal{D}) \rfloor$), $\ell(q)$ the prefix-hit length of request $q$ looked up once ($\delta_q$ flag) only if $\kappa(q) \in \mathcal{A}$, $t_{\mathrm{queue}}(q)$ its entry time; key $$p(q) = \begin{cases}(0, -\ell(q), t_{\mathrm{queue}}(q)) & \kappa(q) \in \mathcal{A}\\ (1, 0, t_{\mathrm{queue}}(q)) & \kappa(q) \notin \mathcal{A}\end{cases}$$ sorted ascending lexicographically, then SGLang's batch builder. Priority-computation time over a batch (Table 1): SWE at $C_S = 289$: LPM 735.00 s, DFS-weight 1704.25 s, RP 303.05 s; BFCL at 1950: 7.65 / 172.15 / 10.91 s (LPM falls back to FCFS above a 128-request queue); WideSearch at 200: 62.82 / 144.08 / 39.97 s. Routing (sec. 5.2.3, two TP4 workers): LBCH makespan $1.5$-$13.6\%$ below SGLang cache-aware routing and $1.9$-$3.8\%$ below plain consistent hashing at equal cache reuse ($98.4$-$98.8\%$ SWE, $86.2$-$87.2\%$ BFCL, $95.2$-$95.7\%$ WideSearch); imbalance metrics $\beta = \frac{1}{|J|}\int_J d(t)\,dt$ with $d(t) = |N_1(t) - N_2(t)|/(N_1(t)+N_2(t))$ over intervals $J$ with more than one in-flight request (eqs. 17-18) and $\gamma_{\mathrm{out}} = |D_1 - D_2|/(D_1 + D_2)$ on output tokens (eq. 20). Capacity separation (sec. 4.1): unified harness gate $C_S^{\mathrm{unified}} = \min\{C_I^{\star}, C_E\}$ (eq. 11) versus decoupled $C_S^{\mathrm{decoupled}} = C_I^{\star}$ (eq. 12) with running environment jobs capped at $C_E$ separately; a sample holds its slot from admission to completion, pending jobs hold a sample slot but no execution slot. CAAS (sec. 4.2): for pending environment job $j$ with slot-request time $a_j$, $n_j$ completed inference turns in its trajectory (the turn that produced $j$ included), $\tau_m$ the observed duration of its $m$-th inference turn, band width $B$ and bucket width $\Delta_I$: $$g_j = \lfloor a_j / B \rfloor, \quad \bar\tau_j = \frac{1}{n_j}\sum_{m=1}^{n_j} \tau_m, \quad c_j = \lceil \bar\tau_j / \Delta_I \rceil,$$ (eqs. 13-15) and the fixed key $$p_E(j) = (g_j,\ -n_j,\ c_j,\ e_j)$$ (eq. 16), $e_j$ a global entry sequence, sorted ascending: earlier arrival band first, then deeper revealed chain, then shorter mean inference time, then FCFS. 'Observed progress' is therefore $n_j$ alone, a count of completed turns; no remaining-length estimate, no per-task history. $B = 30$ s, $\Delta_I = 1$ s everywhere (App. A.2, A.3). Tail metric (eq. 21): $t_q$ the time the completed fraction first reaches $q\%$, $L_p = t_{100} - t_{100-p}$. Replay results on MCP-Atlas (sec. 5.3; 495 recorded trajectories, two TP4 workers, $r = 0.14$, FCFS job order unless stated): raising $C_S$ from the unified value ($C_S = C_E$) to 10 cuts makespan by about one third at both $C_E = 3$ and $C_E = 5$; $C_S = 25$ and $50$ are flat; CAAS versus FCFS at $C_S = 50$: makespan $-1.9\%$ ($C_E = 3$), $-3.5\%$ ($C_E = 5$); $L_5$ $-19.0\%$ and $-21.4\%$ while CAAS reaches 95% completion later (Fig. 12). Live inference-side (Table 2, mean of three runs, makespan in minutes): Ling-3.0-Flash BFCL 68.4 to 49.2 ($-28.1\%$), SWE Baseline-1 166.9 / Baseline-2 197.7 / Opt 149.5 ($-10.4\%$ against the tuned baseline, $-24.4\%$ against the concurrency-matched one), WideSearch 186.7 to 116.7 ($-37.5\%$); Ling-3.1-Flash SWE 234.1 / 304.1 / 185.1 ($-20.9\%$, $-39.1\%$), WideSearch 459.9 to 359.1 ($-21.9\%$). Cache reuse on SWE: 98.3 / 87.5 / 98.6% (3.0) and 98.2 / 80.4 / 98.3% (3.1); new-prefill tokens 22.2M / 170.9M / 19.0M and 19.3M / 211.8M / 17.9M (Table A3). Live MCP-Atlas (Table 3, three 500-task runs each, baseline $C_S = C_E = 3$, Opt $C_S = 50$, $C_E = 3$): Ling-3.0-Flash Baseline 466.1 min, Opt-FCFS 168.2 ($-63.9\%$), Opt-CAAS 163.0 ($-3.1\%$ versus Opt-FCFS; $-65.0\%$ versus baseline); $L_5$ 38.9 / 67.6 / 66.0 min, $L_{10}$ 73.7 / 79.2 / 73.4 min; mean in-flight inference calls 1.2 / 7.3 / 7.9; scores 65.5 / 66.6 / 65.6. Ling-3.1-Flash 333.5 / 140.5 / 128.5 min ($-57.9\%$; CAAS $-8.5\%$ versus FCFS); $L_5$ 26.1 / 49.8 / 35.3, $L_{10}$ 43.5 / 54.4 / 38.6; in-flight 1.6 / 12.5 / 11.5; scores 81.0 / 80.9 / 81.3. The final 25 tasks under Opt-CAAS average 27.9 (3.0) and 15.6 (3.1) turns against 10.1 and 7.9 under the baseline (sec. 5.4). Derived from Table 3, not stated by the paper: after capacity separation the last 5% of tasks occupy $L_5/t_{100} = 66.0/163.0 = 40\%$ (3.0) and $35.3/128.5 = 27\%$ (3.1) of the makespan, against 8% under the baseline.
load_bearing_assumption: Two proxies stand in for information the scheduler does not have, and the paper names both. (1) One workload-mean footprint predicts live residency pressure: 'This balancing ratio may not be optimal in practice, since the workload-wide mean KV-cache footprint may not reflect the cache demand of the trajectories active at a given time.' (sec. 3.1.2); 'Because the accumulated context generally grows across turns, the final-turn KV-cache allocation provides a conservative workload estimate, although it is not treated as a strict upper bound.' (sec. 3.1.1); the ratio is then frozen: 'The selected ratio $\hat r$ stays fixed during inference serving.' (sec. 3.1.2). The measured best ratios differ from $r^{\mathrm{bal}}$ by $0.5$-$1.5\times$ and the paper never reports how much makespan that costs. (2) Completed turns predict remaining turns: 'With future trajectory lengths unknown, CAAS uses completed inference turns as a proxy for potentially long trajectories' (sec. 4.2). No distribution of chain lengths $N_k$ is reported for any workload, so the strength of the proxy (how well $n_j$ ranks remaining work) is unknown (not in text); the only evidence is that the Opt-CAAS tail tasks 'also require more turns in baseline runs' when matched by task id (sec. 5.4). (3) For the replay harness, that environment service time is independent of dispatch order and concurrency: 'Stage dependencies and environment durations remain fixed, while inference latency and cache reuse arise from actual serving.' (sec. 5.1), while the live environments are the ones that 'may degrade under high concurrency or encounter upstream rate limits such as HTTP 429 errors' (App. A.2), which is the reason $C_E$ exists.
weakest_component: The baseline behind the headline. (1) The $65.0\%$ on MCP-Atlas is against a harness running three tasks at a time: 'the baseline uses unified admission with $C_S = C_E = 3$' (App. A.3), with mean in-flight inference calls of 1.2 (3.0) and 1.6 (3.1) on eight and sixteen H20 GPUs (Table 3); raising $C_S$ to 50 with FCFS does $63.9\%$ and $57.9\%$ of it, and the paper's own replay shows $C_S = 10$ already captures about a third and $C_S = 25$ to $50$ is flat (sec. 5.3). The scheduling contribution, CAAS, is $1.9$-$3.5\%$ in replay and $3.1$-$8.5\%$ live. (2) Three runs, no spread: every live number is 'averaged equally over three runs per configuration' (Table 2, 3) with no standard deviation, range or test, while 'Stochastic model sampling and environment variability cause trajectories and token counts to differ across live runs' (sec. 5.4); the CAAS live gain of $5.2$ min on a $168$ min batch (3.0) is within what one slow MCP server could do. (3) 'Scores remain aligned' is never defined: deltas are $+2.65$ (BFCL), $+0.2$ / $+1.17$ (SWE), $-0.9$ / $-0.5$ (WideSearch), $+0.1$ / $+0.3$ (MCP-Atlas) points, three runs each, no interval. (4) The capacity model is validated by closeness to a grid search whose values are only in a figure ('close to the best measured values', sec. 5.2.1); at the best BFCL ratio the reference concurrency $C_{\mathrm{ref}} = 859$ is the upper edge of the collapse band ($644$-$859$, Fig. 4), i.e. the model's operating point sits where reuse breaks. (5) Comparisons are matched in GPU count and engine (same SGLang, same hardware, same checkpoint within each row) and the baselines' concurrency is tuned 'targeting GPU saturation without substantial inference queueing' (sec. 5.4), which is fair; but only SWE has a concurrency-matched Baseline-2, so on BFCL and WideSearch the $28$-$37\%$ cannot be split between 'more concurrency' and 'better cache policy'; the baselines keep SGLang's default cache ratio 0.9 against the Opt ratios 0.1-1.5 (Table A2), so part of the gain is a default nobody tuned for this model. (6) Live routing imbalance $\beta$ worsens under Opt (BFCL 10.6 to 17.0, WideSearch 11.5 to 15.6 and 8.8 to 17.6, Table 2), the opposite of the replay routing result. (7) The replay set is survivors only: 'only successful historical executions were collected; failed executions were excluded' (App. A.1), so the tail of failing or retrying trajectories that live makespan includes is absent from every ablation.
regime: Models: Ling-3.0-Flash (124B total, 5.1B active; Kimi Delta Attention and Multi-head Latent Attention layers at 5:1, sparse MoE) and Ling-3.1-Flash (560B total, 25B active), both with thinking enabled and 256K maximum context (App. A.3). Engine: SGLang (RadixAttention prefix cache, mamba_full_memory_ratio, path-based Mamba-state eviction with one state per path), the authors' LBCH router policy and RP scheduler policy added. Hardware: NVIDIA H20; replay on one or two TP4 workers; live on two TP4 workers over eight H20 (3.0) and two TP8 workers over sixteen H20 (3.1). Workloads (Table A1, A2): SWE-bench Multilingual, 289 recorded successful trajectories / 25,416 requests / 6.0M output tokens in replay, 300 live tasks; BFCL-v4, 5,106 trajectories / 17,029 requests (includes single-turn), live only for 3.0; WideSearch, 200 trajectories / 5,672 requests / 4.7M output tokens; MCP-Atlas, 495 recorded trajectories in replay, 500 live tasks, external MCP services with the official runner defaulting to five concurrent tasks. Concurrency: $C_S$ swept 98-2000 in replay; live baselines $C_S = 100 / 100 / 40 / 3$ (3.0) and $50 / 100 / 15 / 3$ (3.1), Opt $300 / 250 / 100 / 50$ and $100 / 40 / 50$; environment capacity $C_E \in \{3, 5\}$ in replay, 3 live; baseline cache ratio 0.9 throughout, Opt ratios 0.1-1.5. Horizon: 'long contexts and deep chains' on SWE (App. A.1), final-25 MCP-Atlas tasks average 8-28 turns; no chain-length distribution reported. Makespans 49 min to 7.7 h; live timeouts six and thirteen hours in replay. Runs: three per live configuration; replay points are single batches. Pass-rate band: scores 65.5-88.3 (Tables 2-3). Dollar cost and total GPU-hours: unknown (not in text). Venue: cs.DC preprint 2026-11-12, Ling Team, Ant Group; the methods are stated to be in production for Ling-3.x training and evaluation.
information_asymmetry: At admission the harness knows the submission order, one workload-mean final-turn footprint $L_{\mathrm{kv}}(\mathcal{D})$ from an earlier checkpoint, and the caps $C_S$, $C_E$; it does not know a trajectory's turn count $N_k$, its context growth or its tool durations. As the chain runs it reveals $n_j$ and the inference times $\tau_m$, and CAAS uses exactly those two (eq. 16). Three pieces of information exist elsewhere and are never used. (1) The replay harness holds every job's recorded service time and every trajectory's stage sequence before the run starts ('recorded environment responses and durations', sec. 5.1), so a hindsight-optimal dispatch on known $N_k$ and durations is computable offline; CAAS is compared with FCFS only, never with that bound, so how much tail any ordering can remove is unknown. CL-W43-08 asks the same question of a different rule; CAAS is a second observation-only rule in print with no capture ratio. (2) The same tasks recur across checkpoints (sec. 1) and the authors show long-tail tasks are long in the baseline too ('When matched by task ID, the Opt-CAAS tail tasks also require more turns in baseline runs', sec. 5.4), so a per-task prior on $N_k$ sits in their logs; CAAS is built 'without requiring sample-specific historical profiles' (sec. 4.2), and the gap between the progress proxy and that prior is unmeasured. (3) Only makespan and mean in-flight calls are measured; per-sample GPU-seconds, environment-slot idle time, GPU idle fraction and the chain-length distribution are not, so the tail's cost shows only in the derived $L_5/t_{100}$ of 27-40%. In RL rollouts the trainer also knows which trajectories matter (advantage, staleness) and can abandon a tail instead of racing it; here every sample is owed. Ideas come from the tail share, the missing oracle bound, and the three-task harness default the field's baselines inherit.
occupies: Published and not claimable: the closed-form balancing ratio $r^{\mathrm{bal}} = F_{\mathrm{state}}/F_{\mathrm{kv}}(\mathcal{D})$ and reference concurrency $W\lfloor M/(F_{\mathrm{kv}} + F_{\mathrm{state}})\rfloor$ for splitting SGLang's KV and recurrent-state pools on a hybrid model from historical trajectory footprints, with the finding that reuse collapses and new-prefill work rises 3-11$\times$ past a ratio-dependent concurrency; per-turn load-bounded consistent hashing on a trajectory label (LBCH, $\alpha = 1.25$) and the two-tier routing-prefix queue sort that runs the radix lookup once per request only for recently batched trajectories; separating the sample-admission cap from the environment-execution cap in an agent harness (and the observation that MCP-Atlas and $\tau$-bench harnesses use one gate); CAAS, the fixed key (arrival band, $-$completed turns, inference-time bucket, FCFS) on pending tool jobs, and its numbers (replay $1.9$-$3.5\%$ makespan, $19$-$21\%$ $L_5$; live $3.1$-$8.5\%$); the replay harness design (real inference, recorded tool responses and durations, recorded output lengths); the live 10.4-65.0% table on Ling-3.x with H20 SGLang. Left open by the paper's own text: hierarchical (host-tier) caching and eviction policies for hybrid models, makespan under TTFT/TPOT SLOs, parallel sub-agent workflows, any oracle or remaining-length-aware dispatch, failed and retried trajectories in replay, chain-length distributions, variance across runs, and any engine other than SGLang or model other than Ling.

neighbors.title: ARL-Tangram: Unleash the Resource Efficiency in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
neighbors.trick: Treat each tool action in agentic RL as a schedulable unit, pick candidates FCFS and elastically resize the CPU/GPU slice each gets to minimise summed action completion time, sharing external resources across trajectories instead of pinning them; the paper's closest environment-side neighbour, differing in that CAAS reorders jobs under a fixed slot count and does not change service times (sec. 2).

neighbors.title: Autellix: An Efficient Serving Engine for LLM Agents as General Programs
neighbors.trick: Intercept an agent program's LLM calls and preempt or prioritise them by how much service the program has already received, so short programs are not blocked behind long ones; the paper's scheduling neighbour, from which RP differs by using recent-batch labels rather than attained service, and CAAS by ordering tool jobs rather than LLM calls (sec. 2).

neighbors.title: SAGA: Workflow-Atomic Scheduling for AI Agent Inference on GPU Clusters
neighbors.trick: Schedule the whole agent workflow as one unit, predict KV reuse across tool calls from an execution graph and expected tool durations (within 1.31x of Belady), and batch by session affinity with work stealing; the paper's prediction-based neighbour, against which LBCH and RP use only a trajectory label and no workflow graph (sec. 2).

neighbors.title: Idleness is Relative: Exploiting Tool-Call Idle Windows for Offloading in Agentic Systems with MORI
neighbors.trick: Rank agent programs by their recent fraction of time inside tool calls, keep the least idle in GPU memory, the next tier in CPU DRAM, and drop the rest, with admission at both tiers; the paper's environment-aware cache neighbour, which uses tool idleness to place cache where this paper uses chain depth to order tool jobs (sec. 2).

neighbors.title: Asymmetric Virtual Memory Paging for Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Inference
neighbors.trick: Give KV cache and SSM state physically separate pools behind one virtual address space and migrate capacity between them only when an allocation fails, cutting OOM events and padding waste on hybrid models; the paper's hybrid-cache neighbour, which adapts the split at runtime where this paper fixes it before serving from a workload profile (sec. 2).

theme_fit.why: rollout-engine scheduling, prefix and recurrent-state reuse under concurrency, the environment-capacity bottleneck and the chain tail, and the cost structure of batched agent workloads are the lane sentence verbatim; it is a second observation-only scheduling rule in print with no oracle or capture ratio, the shape CL-W43-08 is built on, and its derived tail share (final 5% of tasks = 27-40% of makespan after capacity separation) is a cost-structure datum the lane lacks

same words (benchmark harness, MCP-Atlas, SWE-bench, score alignment), different problem: it shows that harness concurrency defaults (three tasks at a time) set benchmark run cost, and that 'scores remain aligned' is undefined, but measures no agent

RL rollouts are named as the workload and the methods are said to run in Ling-3.x training, but no training signal, staleness or sample value enters the scheduler; the RL analogue (shed or truncate the tail by advantage) is not in the paper

limitations_as_complaints: My cache split is one scalar per workload, fixed before the run, from the mean final-turn footprint of trajectories on an earlier checkpoint, and I know it is not the live demand: 'This balancing ratio may not be optimal in practice, since the workload-wide mean KV-cache footprint may not reflect the cache demand of the trajectories active at a given time. Optional local calibration can identify a better-performing nearby ratio.' (sec. 3.1.2); 'The selected ratio $\hat r$ stays fixed during inference serving.' (sec. 3.1.2). My best measured ratios were 0.5-1.5x my formula's and I never say what that gap costs in minutes; hierarchical caching and hybrid-model eviction are future work (sec. 6).

My tail scheduler knows only how many turns a chain has completed, not how many remain, and the tail is now most of the batch: 'With future trajectory lengths unknown, CAAS uses completed inference turns as a proxy for potentially long trajectories' (sec. 4.2); 'Although CAAS reaches 95% completion later, it finishes the batch earlier.' (sec. 5.3); 'The final 25 tasks under Opt-CAAS average 27.9 and 15.6 turns ... compared with 10.1 and 7.9 under the baseline.' (sec. 5.4). I never compare against a hindsight-optimal order even though my replay harness holds every recorded duration, I never report the chain-length distribution, and I get 1.9-3.5% in replay.

My controlled ablations replay only successful trajectories with frozen tool durations, while the live environments I am protecting slow down with concurrency and my live numbers are three-run means with no spread: 'only successful historical executions were collected; failed executions were excluded' and 'it does not evaluate semantic correctness or cover all failures and retries' (App. A.1); 'Stage dependencies and environment durations remain fixed' (sec. 5.1); 'MCP-Atlas tasks depend on external MCP services, which may degrade under high concurrency or encounter upstream rate limits such as HTTP 429 errors.' (App. A.2); 'Stochastic model sampling and environment variability cause trajectories and token counts to differ across live runs.' (sec. 5.4). Makespan under TTFT/TPOT SLOs is also open (sec. 6).
